seriesTitle: The Reckoner of the Thirteenth Hour
title: Chapter 7: Three Hours Owed
blurb: Petra learns where the seconds come from, and Tran's debt of sleep comes due on the plate.

blocks.text: The card was still on my blotter when Drewe came up the night stair. I had not put it back in the drawer, and I had not put it anywhere else.
She set the snuffbox down beside it. Then she saw the card, and her hand stopped halfway back to her pocket.
'That's his hand,' she said. 'Same as the lid cards. Same round letters.'
'Mabry's.'
'Mabry's.' She turned the card with one finger until it faced her. 'He's never written a whole sentence on one before. It's always times.'

I had found it at twenty to two that morning in a locked drawer, and the Guild holds the only other key to that drawer. Mabry is not the Guild. Someone had carried his card through a door he could not open himself.

My verdict was that the card meant my father. Orme had read his file and told me so with a line about untidy logs. Now Mabry knew it too, and wanted me to know he knew. That was why the post had gone to Orme. I had believed it since the day he took the desk, and now the card said it in a stranger's hand. I did not say any of this to Drewe.
'Hold it,' she said, and pushed the box across the blotter to me. 'Properly. Bare hand. Tell me what you hear.'
'Hear.'
'Couriers say a warm one remembers where it came from, if you're patient. Most people put it down after ten seconds.' She looked at the desk clock. 'It isn't in your printed Laws.'
It was not. I had read them through. I took it as courier talk, and I picked up the box.

I held it for a full minute by the desk clock. There was nothing but warm brass in my palm and the hinge pressing my thumb. Drewe did not fidget. It was the first time I had seen her hands keep still.
Then I heard a tram bell.

It did not come from the window. The window was shut and the street under it was quiet. The bell was in my hand with the brass, and it rang once, a little way off, the way a stop's bell sounds when the tram is still round the corner.
After the bell my feet were cold. They were in boots under a desk beside the stove, and they were cold, as if I had been standing on stone for a quarter of an hour.
After that I wanted to look at a clock. I wanted it the way you want to scratch. I looked up at the desk clock, and it was not the clock I wanted.
I put the box down. The cold went out of my feet slowly.
'A tram stop,' I said. 'Somebody standing in the cold, waiting, watching a clock.'
Drewe nodded. 'That's what I get. Every time. Bells, and wanting the time.'

The printed Laws say a warm second is drawn by catch-brass from a living person's waiting, and stays warm for a day. They do not say where the brass is. I thought of the clock at the Guild Hall stop, two minutes behind my watch, and the queue under it longer than the timetable explained. I thought of forty sealed orders in the cabinet behind me, every one headed 'Public clock, maintenance'.

'He asked why it came back full after the Regulars,' Drewe said. 'I told him their Arbiter watched our bench all night. He said that was very sensible of me and gave me a sugared almond. Then he took it in the back and brought it out like that.' She put five coins on the blotter, new ones. 'He paid. I'm not spending it.'
'You went back.'

'I'm going to keep going back.' She kept her eyes on the box. 'I carry it, I take his card, I wind nothing. Every match you get a full box to listen to and his times in his own hand. I'm the escapement now. It ticks, and nothing goes anywhere.'
'And the others?'

'Asked them on the landing at six. Marguerite said yes before I'd finished. Tran said mm, and then he said yes properly, because I made him.' She looked up. 'It's my box. It's my name if it goes wrong. I'm not asking you to carry it.'

I wanted to tell her no. I wanted it to be mine to decide, so that if it went wrong it would be my report and my fault. It was not mine to decide. She had already decided it, and the team had already agreed.
'Yes,' I said.
'Then watch this,' Drewe said, 'so you know it when somebody else does it.'

She came round the end of the desk. Her right hand went into her coat pocket and stayed there. Her left hand took my wrist, lightly, her thumb on the inside of it, the way you steady somebody who has stood up too fast.
'That's all it is,' she said. 'Box in the pocket, fingers on the lid. Other hand on the wrist. Anyone watching sees me being kind.'
'How long?'
'About as long as it takes to say "steady, you're all right".'
Her fingers on my wrist were dry and light. She wound nothing; she was showing me. If I had not been watching for it I would have taken it for kindness.
She let go and went back round the desk.

I picked up the box. It was still warm. I could have locked it in the drawer with my key. I could have taken it to the Bank in the morning and told them all of it, and that would have been honest, and it would have ended her.
I held it out to her. It was her risk to carry, and mine to let her carry it.
Drewe put it in her coat. She left the coins.
'What will you do about that?' she said, and nodded at the card.
'Nothing yet.'
I put the card inside my notebook, against the back cover. When she had gone I put my key in the drawer, as I do on nights without a match, and locked it.

At four the next afternoon I did the Night Audit filing, as I have every afternoon since Orme moved it to me. When it was done I did not go down for tea. I took the public-clock register off the shelf behind the cabinets.

The Guild keeps a line for every public clock it winds: its number, where it stands, its movement, and the number of the last order that touched it. Night staff may read it. I had used it a hundred times to check winders' timesheets.
I opened my notebook at the inside cover, where I had written the forty order numbers, and began with the Guild Hall ward, because I can see that stop from my tram.
The ward has six public clocks. Five carried order numbers I did not know. The sixth was the pillar clock at the Guild Hall tram stop. Its last order was the ninth number on my cover.
I checked it against the cover digit by digit, and then against the register again. It was the same number.

That order was in the closed cabinet a few feet from my chair, under its seal, signed C. Orme like the other thirty-nine. By Guild rule I could not open it without the Senior Night Auditor's written instruction. The Senior Night Auditor was Orme.
I did not know what the order said. I knew the clock it touched ran two minutes slow, and that the queue under it was longer than the timetable explained. I knew what I had felt in my feet.

There was no time for the other wards before the night desk. I wrote 'Guild Hall stop: order on cover, ninth' in my notebook and put the register back on its shelf, spine out, square with the others, the way I had found it.
On the second afternoon I went to the League office over the east gate to lodge our sheet for training night.

The Ropewalk Stair's Reckoner was at the counter ahead of me. Askew is a tall woman with a clean collar and ink along the side of her right hand, which means she writes a great deal and does not wait for it to dry. We play Ropewalk on matchday eleven. It is the last match of the Turn.
She stepped aside to let me reach the counter, which she did not have to do.
'Miss Sandor,' she said. 'I watched your side at Millrace, and again against Bellpull. I've been wondering how your players are always so fresh.'
Her voice was pleasant. Her hands were folded on top of her gloves on the counter, and they did not move.
I said nothing. I gave the clerk my sheet.

'Your Sprinter spends two hundred a match,' Askew said, 'and she walks up to the Arbiter's table a week later as if she'd slept like a child. Mine spend half that and come to me grey. Some of them stall on the stairs.'
I signed the slip the clerk pushed at me.
Askew smiled at me as if I had told her something. Then she picked up her gloves and went down the stair.

My verdict was that I had. A Reckoner who asks that question already has half the answer, and when she gets silence back she can work out the other half. Whatever she did with it, she would have done it by matchday eleven.
I took my key out of the drawer at half past eleven. Nothing else in the drawer had moved.

Training night is sixty seconds for the week, no scoring, and the same debts as a match. Marguerite had booked every one of them. She had written the drills out on the back of a pie-shop bill: drill, plate, spend, one under another, with the last eleven seconds kept back 'for whatever goes wrong'.
'Every second's got a home,' she said, and slapped the bill down on the bench. 'You book it, I say yes to every line, nobody stalls on a stair. Good, isn't it? Say it's good.'
'It's good.'
'It's brilliant. I'll take good. Tran, wake up, she said it's good.'
Tran was on the bench with the stone jug of black chicory between his boots and his eyes shut. He opened them before she reached him.
'Heard,' he said. 'Mm. Brilliant.'

There is no Arbiter on a training night and no sleep ledger to fill in. The last one Tran had filled in was at the MD10 check, and I had been standing beside him. He wrote his line with his eyes on the stair door, as he had at Millrace and at the Bellpull check, and he did not look at the page afterwards. He had asked me for the Rate Board, the Regulars' sheet and the time of the Close that week. He had not asked for my copy of the ledger.
The Regulator struck below us, and we were in the Hour. The stair window behind plate VI showed the city stopped at midnight, as it always does.
I stood on the Arbor with the training jar.

Drill one was live, no spends. Marguerite walked the Token round from IX with Drewe a plate ahead of her as the screen, and Tran kept XII. He opened his Still at half as soon as Marguerite stepped on to XI. When she came on to XII she moved like someone wading. Tran walked across the plate at his own pace, put a hand on her shoulder, and she set the Token down.
'Again,' Marguerite said.

With four of us there was nobody to put on the plates between IX and XII. Tran had to hold the whole Keep himself, every drill, and hold it early. I wrote the start and end of each of his Stills on my sheet, because every minute of Still time is an hour of Still-sleep owed inside two days.
Drill two was a spend. 'Lisle, eight,' I said.
'Held.'

She said, 'Spend eight,' and I was frozen. When I could see again she was on the rim of XII with the Token in her hand, Drewe was standing where Marguerite had been, and Tran had a hand on Marguerite's arm.
'After,' Tran said. 'She came in a step short. Mm.'
'I booked that step,' Marguerite said. 'I'll book a longer one.' She laughed and walked the Token back to IX.
Drills three and four went the same way, a step closer each time. Tran held his Still open through all of it. By the end of drill four my sheet had him at a little over three minutes.
'That's three hours of sleep owed inside two days,' I told him while Marguerite reset. 'Can you sleep it?'
'Sleep's my best event,' he said. 'Ask the bench.'
'He's the only man I know,' Drewe said, 'who could nap through a striking train.'
Tran drank from the jug. His hand on the handle was steady. His eyes were red at the rims. He had held the Keep on his own for four matches because there were four of us and no one else to do it.
My verdict was that he was tired from carrying us. I meant to give him a lighter week before MD11, with no long Stills in it that a sheet could spare him, and I meant to tell him so after the drills.

Drill five was Marguerite's longest. 'Lisle, twelve,' I said. 'Held.' She said 'Spend twelve,' and I was frozen, and when I could see again she was on XI, square to XII, with the Token in both hands and her spend gone. She stepped on to XII in live play. Tran's Still was open. She waded.
Tran did not walk across the plate.
He stood where he had stood all night, at the centre, with his hands at his sides. His chin went down.
'Come on,' Marguerite said. 'I'm right here. Get me.'

He did not move. She set the Token down herself and reached for his shoulder, and her arm went out at half the speed it should have, because the plate was still at half. Her hand closed on his shoulder and shook it. His head rolled and came back upright. His eyes stayed shut.
I was afraid.

I watched Marguerite's hands. The right one held his shoulder. The left one came up slowly and took his collar, and both of them shook him, and the cloth bunched in her fingers and smoothed out again. A teammate's hand does not Shake a Still. Only an opponent's does.
'Bao,' Drewe said from the rim of XI. Then louder: 'Bao.'
Marguerite let go of his collar and patted his cheek, slowly. Her mouth was open. She had gone quiet.
Tran slept on his feet in the middle of plate XII with his Still held, and the plate crawled on at half around him, and none of us could wake him.
